title: Mutual Funds
outcomes: Explain mutual funds, their benefits and drawbacks.
Classify funds and describe scheme types.
Compute NAV and returns; explain loads, expense ratio, side pocketing and tracking error.
Evaluate funds and the role of managers and FPIs.

meta.exam_tip: Mutual fund sums usually test NAV, returns with distributions, and loads.

concepts.title: What mutual funds are and how they work
body: A mutual fund pools money from many investors and invests it in securities according to a stated objective, managed by an asset management company (AMC) under a trust structure regulated by SEBI. Investors hold units whose value moves with the fund's net asset value.

Benefits: professional management, diversification, liquidity, low cost of entry, transparency, regulation and convenience (SIPs, switches). Drawbacks: costs and fees, no control over holdings, possible underperformance, over-diversification and tax or exit-load frictions.
Individuals, HUFs, companies, trusts, NRIs and institutions can invest. Direct plans (bought without distributors) carry lower expense ratios than regular plans.
concepts.analogy: Pool the money, hire a professional, share the results.
concepts.work: A ₹500 monthly SIP gives a small investor a diversified portfolio.

concepts.title: Classification and types of schemes
body: By structure: open-ended (continuous buying and redemption), close-ended (fixed maturity, listed) and interval funds. By portfolio: equity, debt (gilt, liquid, income, money market), hybrid/balanced and special funds (index, sector, thematic, international, fund of funds).

Types of schemes: diversified equity, ELSS (tax-saving with lock-in), sector and thematic funds, arbitrage funds (exploit cash-futures price differences), hedge funds, cash funds, exchange-traded funds (trade on exchanges like shares, track an index or commodity such as gold), and fixed maturity plans (closed-ended debt with set tenure).
By ownership: public sector, private sector and foreign-sponsored AMCs.
concepts.analogy: Match the scheme to the goal and horizon.
concepts.work: An ETF tracking Nifty trades on the exchange throughout the day.

concepts.title: NAV, loads, expense ratio, side pocketing and tracking error
body: Net asset value (NAV) per unit = (market value of investments + other assets − liabilities including accrued expenses) ÷ units outstanding. Holding-period return = (closing NAV − opening NAV + distributions) ÷ opening NAV.

Entry loads are not charged in India (abolished by SEBI); exit loads may apply on early redemption. Trail commission is paid to distributors over time. The expense ratio (annual expenses ÷ average net assets) reduces returns and is capped by SEBI.

Side pocketing segregates a stressed or downgraded debt security into a separate portfolio, protecting other investors and allowing recovery to be shared fairly. Tracking error is the standard deviation of the difference between fund and benchmark returns — the key quality measure for index funds and ETFs.
concepts.analogy: NAV is net assets per unit; costs and tracking error eat into it.
concepts.work: A downgraded bond moved into a side pocket stops it dragging down main NAV.

concepts.title: Evaluating funds and the role of managers
body: Quantitative evaluation: absolute and relative returns versus benchmark and peers, risk-adjusted measures (Sharpe, Treynor, Jensen's alpha), expense ratio, tracking error, portfolio turnover and fund size.
Qualitative evaluation: fund house reputation, manager track record and stability, investment process, portfolio quality and concentration, and service.

Actively managed funds aim to beat a benchmark through selection and timing; passively managed funds aim to replicate an index at low cost. FPIs (earlier FIIs) influence market liquidity and flows and can invest via mutual funds and directly.
concepts.analogy: Judge a fund on risk-adjusted returns, costs and the people behind it.
concepts.work: A passive fund wins if its costs and tracking error stay very low.

illustrations.title: NAV and holding-period return
illustrations.q: Growth Plus Fund holds securities worth ₹520 crore at market value and has liabilities (including accrued expenses) of ₹20 crore; 25 crore units are outstanding. NAV a year ago was ₹18 and a dividend of ₹1 per unit was paid during the year. Compute NAV, the investor's return, and the redemption price with a 1% exit load.

illustrations.title: Tracking error of an index fund
illustrations.q: Over four quarters, an index fund's returns minus its benchmark's returns were +0.2%, −0.1%, +0.3% and −0.2%. Compute the tracking error (standard deviation of differences, using n − 1). What does a high tracking error indicate?

jobs.situation: A client wants a long-term equity fund and a short-term parking option.
steps: Match objective and horizon to scheme type.

jobs.takeaway: Costs and consistency often matter more than last year's winner.
